doc.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Band dynamics in BS&T and Lipsius as creative force
summary: Life on the road, a cooperative band without a leader, and Lipsius's arrangements being rejected.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: That’s good. Was Blood, Sweat & Tears a difficult group as far as — some rock bands have personalities that constantly—

Well let’s put it this way. Marriage is not an easy thing for people, to live together for years. And married people usually the husband goes out and he’s working all day and in today’s world sometimes the wife too. And you only see each other for a few hours at night and a few hours in the morning. When you’re in a band and you’re on the road, you are with these guys night and day, four or five days a week. And when you take a trip you’re with them night and day seven days a week, except when you’re sleeping. So naturally personalities are going to grate on each other. It also was a cooperative band which means that the only way to emerge as a leader over a cooperative band is by using all kinds of political techniques that are used. It’s a bit ugly but it’s the only way that somebody can emerge as a leader is by gathering the votes of others or this or that. There was no leader per se. There was no leader, so some more aggressive personalities emerged as bosses and squelched some of the more creative personalities that were more passive. And I’m not even talking about myself, of course I felt it only in playing the

same tunes over and over again, becoming prisoners of our own hits. Whereas what I’m saying is the real creative forces in that band was a particular arranger to me named Lipsius. I mean Halligan also, but Lipsius was the prime creative arranger in the band. And he is kind of a shy, laid back sort. And oh man, he would bring in this chart or that chart and instead of saying okay we’ll do this, okay we’ll record this, it was like naaa that’s no good, naaa that’s no good. And finally he just stopped.
Yeah, he had less arrangements on those records than he should have.
